## Core difference

Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but they do it differently:

- **Merge** creates a new commit that ties together two histories. Nothing is rewritten — every existing commit stays exactly as it was, and you get a merge commit with two parents.
- **Rebase** replays your branch's commits one by one on top of another branch's tip, producing new commits (new hashes) with the same changes. History ends up linear, as if you'd branched off later than you actually did.

## Practical implications

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History shape | Branching, preserves what actually happened | Linear, rewrites what happened |
| Commit identity | Unchanged | New commits (new SHAs) |
| Safe on shared/pushed branches? | Yes | No — rewriting public history breaks collaborators' clones |
| Conflict resolution | Once, at merge time | Potentially once per replayed commit |
| Traceability | Shows exactly when branches diverged/joined | Loses that context, but reads cleanly |

## When to reach for each

**Merge:**
- Integrating a feature branch into `main`/`develop`, especially anything already pushed/shared
- You want an audit trail of when work actually landed
- Working with others on the same branch

**Rebase:**
- Cleaning up your own local, not-yet-pushed commits before opening a PR (squash/reorder/fix messages)
- Keeping a feature branch up to date with `main` as it moves, so the eventual merge is trivial (`git rebase main` on your branch, then merge/fast-forward)
- You want a clean, linear history for `git bisect` or easy review

**Rule of thumb:** rebase what's private and not yet shared; merge (never rebase) what's already public/pushed, unless the whole team has agreed to force-push conventions.
